intro: Before you rises the Great Altar of Pergamon, from around 170 to 159 BC. It is less an altar than a stage: the 113-metre Gigantomachy frieze wraps the building in a battle told in stone. Between 1878 and 1886 it was dismantled and shipped to Berlin, so what stands at Pergamon now is the terrace and the footings. In the model, the whole building rises again.
spot-1: Now you are looking at the Gigantomachy frieze: 113 metres of high relief, the gods locked in battle against the giants, wrapping the whole building.
spot-2: Now you are looking at the great stairway. Twenty metres wide, it climbs to the terrace between the two wings. Imagine making that climb yourself.
spot-3: Here you are looking at the colonnade: the Ionic colonnade that runs all the way round the terrace.
spot-4: Now you are looking at the court on top, where the fire altar itself stood. The frieze below was its stage; here was the altar.
spot-5: And now you are looking at one of the wings. Projecting on either side of the stair, the wings carry the frieze round without breaking it.
uncertainty: Finally, an honest word about what this model does not know. The base, the frieze and the width of the stairway are known from excavated blocks. The height of 12 metres comes from an ancient note by Ampelius, and it is disputed. The proportions of the colonnade on top, whether it was roofed, and the detail of the wings are inference. The frieze band carries a photograph of the Gigantomachy as re-erected in the Pergamonmuseum in Berlin: the carving is real, but the model does not show which scene of that 113-metre narrative sat on which face of the building.
